en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Mahāvibhaṅga,
Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Bhūtagāmavagga 14.
The Training Rule on Lodgings.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Now at that time, during the winter season, some monks had prepared lodgings in the open air and were sunning their bodies; when the time for departure was announced, they left without putting them away, nor did they have them put away, and they departed without taking leave.
Consequently, the lodgings became covered with dust.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:

“How indeed can these monks, having prepared lodgings in the open air, depart without either putting them away themselves or having them put away, and depart without informing anyone, leaving the lodgings in disarray? Then those monks, having rebuked them in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … “Is it true, monks, that monks [acted] in the open air …? [The monks replied,] “It is true, Blessed One. … [The Buddha then spoke in detail. … “Monks, this is not proper for you …” [and so on]. … “Therefore, monks, I will lay down a training rule for monks: ‘If a monk, having prepared a bed or chair in the open air, departs without putting it away himself or having it put away, and departs without informing anyone, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. … And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“Whosoever monk, having spread out a bed, a bench, a mattress, or a rug belonging to the Saṅgha in the open air,
or having had it spread out, when departing does not himself put it away, nor have it put away, or departs without asking permission— ”
“...one incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, having stayed outdoors, the monks would bring back their lodgings very early in the morning.
The Blessed One saw those bhikkhus bringing back their lodgings very early in the morning.
Having seen them, on this occasion and in this context, he gave a discourse on the Dhamma and addressed the bhikkhus:

“I allow you, bhikkhus, for eight months during the period when there is no fixed agreement, to leave your lodgings at a place where crows or hawks do not drop dung—whether it be a pavilion or the foot of a tree.”
"But whoever" means whoever such as this ... [as before] ...
"a monk."
...pe... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
"Belonging to the Saṅgha" means it has been given to the Saṅgha and relinquished to them.
A "bed" means four kinds of beds:
one with legs shaped like elephant trunks, one with legs bound together like a bundle, one with legs shaped like crab claws, and one with detachable legs.
A "seat" (pīṭha) means four kinds of seats: one with legs made of wicker, one with legs bound with leather thongs, one with legs shaped like crab claws, and one with detachable legs.
A "cushion" (bhisi) means...
There are five kinds of mattresses: a wool mattress, a cotton mattress, a bark-fiber mattress, a grass mattress, and a leaf mattress.
A "stuffed mattress" (koccha) is one that is bound together with its stuffing wrapped inside, made of either bark-fiber, reed, muñja grass, or pabbaja grass.
"Having spread" means having spread it oneself.
"Having had it spread" means...
Having had another spread out:
if he has it spread by one who is not fully ordained, that person is an impediment for him;
if he has it spread by one who is fully ordained, the one who spreads it is an impediment.
"Going away, he should not even pick it up" means he should not pick it up himself.
"He should not have it picked up" means...
One should not cause another to dig it up.
Or, one should not go without having asked permission:
if a monk goes beyond the distance of a stone’s throw of an average man without asking permission from a monk, a novice, or a monastery attendant, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If, regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha, one perceives it as belonging to the Saṅgha, and having spread it out or caused it to be spread out in the open air, one departs without either picking it up oneself or causing it to be picked up, or goes away without asking permission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha, one is uncertain...

[and so on] ...if, regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha, one perceives it as belonging to an individual, and having spread it out or caused it to be spread out in the open air, one departs without either picking it up oneself or causing it to be picked up, or goes away without asking permission, there is an offense of expiation.
If one spreads out a woolen rug, a bedspread, a floor-covering, a mat, a piece of hide, a foot-wiping cloth,
or a wooden bench in the open air, or causes it to be spread out, and then departs without either putting it away oneself or having it put away,
or goes without asking permission, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an individual's [property] and he perceives it as belonging to the Saṅgha, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an individual's [property] and he is doubtful about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an individual's [property] and he perceives it as an individual's [property], but it belongs to another individual, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense regarding one's own personal property.
There is no offense if one goes after having removed it.
He goes after having had [the robes] removed;
he goes after taking leave;
he goes while drying [them].
It is obstructed by something, in times of distress,
or for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-offender":
the fourth training rule on lodgings is concluded.
